outcomes: Names the piece on a given square before using its rule, with no hint in the prompt
Taps every square that bishop can reach in a crowded position
Stops each diagonal at the first piece in the way: before an own piece, on an enemy piece
Says that a piece on the bishop's own rank or file does not change its moves
Counts how many squares a bishop can reach and treats a low count as a hint that its own pawns are in the way

Capablanca, Chess Fundamentals, sheet Sec. 6-7 (CI-38), paraphrased

steps.text: The piece on e3 is a **bishop**. In a game nobody names a piece for you, so the first job is to say its name to yourself; the name gives you the rule. A bishop slides along **diagonals**, the slanting lines of squares, and it has four of them. The next four boards follow one diagonal each. Compare each with the squares you tapped.

steps.caption: Up and to the right the diagonal is clear: three squares, then the edge.

line.say: The bishop slides three squares to the edge of the board. Empty squares do not stop it.

steps.caption: Up and to the left the diagonal meets a black pawn.

line.say: The bishop takes the pawn and stops on c5. The square b6 behind it stays out of reach.

steps.caption: Down and to the left the diagonal runs into the corner.

line.say: The bishop slides back two squares. Backward is as good as forward for a bishop.

steps.caption: Down and to the right a white piece stands in the way.

line.say: The bishop can step to f2, but g1 holds White's own king, so it must stop one square short.

steps.text: Two stopping rules cover almost everything. A piece of **your own** blocks the line, and the bishop stops one square before it. A piece of **the enemy** blocks it too, but you may capture it and stop there. Squares behind the piece are out of reach this move. [I] A pinned bishop, or one whose king is in check, can have fewer legal moves; a later lesson covers that.

steps.caption: Count the squares before you look: in the middle the bishop reaches thirteen squares along four long lines.

line.say: The bishop crosses two empty squares to g7 in a single move.

steps.caption: Count first: in the corner it has one line, seven squares. The same piece, much less to do.

line.say: All the way across the board in one move, but only along that one line.

steps.text: A bishop in the middle sees four long lines; in a corner it sees one. [H] My conjecture, not a sourced rule: when a bishop reaches very few squares, first look for your own pawns on its diagonals. Test it on the next boards. It says nothing yet about threats.

steps.caption: At the start the bishop on c1 has no move at all. Its neighbours on b2 and d2 are White's own pawns.

line.say: A pawn steps out of the way and opens the bishop's diagonal.
Black answers in the centre with a pawn of his own.
Now the bishop slides out to f4, which was impossible a moment ago.

steps.caption: After 1.d4 d5 the bishop on c1 can reach five squares.

line.say: It slides to the far end of this diagonal, h6.

steps.caption: After the e-pawn moves, the other bishop wakes up as well: five squares for the bishop on f1.

line.say: The bishop swings out along its diagonal toward the black side.
Black develops a knight, a piece we have not yet used.

steps.text: Pawns often start in the bishop's way, so a pawn move can wake a bishop up. Capablanca's advice, as summarised in our notes (*Chess Fundamentals*, paraphrased), is to start with a centre pawn partly because it frees a bishop and the queen. You have just watched it happen twice. [H] A habit worth trying: before moving a bishop, look at what is shutting it in.

steps.caption: Two of its own pawns shut the bishop in completely. No moves.

line.say: Moving one pawn opens a line again.
Black makes a waiting move with the king.
Now the bishop can step out along the diagonal the pawn left.

steps.caption: A busy middlegame position. The bishop on c1 has a line out through d2, because the d-pawn has gone to d3.

line.say: It goes to the edge of its diagonal; nothing of either side stands in the way.
[I] h6 asks the bishop where it will go; it can retreat or take on f6.

steps.title: One change at a time
steps.prompt: Predict the squares in each position before opening the next one. The first is the reference; then one black pawn is added; then a rook moves.

steps.text: Your routine before any bishop move. Say the piece's name. Look along each of its four diagonals. Stop at the first piece in the way: if it is yours, stop one square short; if it is the enemy's, you may land on it. Last, check that the square you want is on your list. Do this out loud for a while; it will become automatic.

steps.caption: A piece directly in front of the bishop, on the same file, blocks nothing. The bishop still reaches the same thirteen squares as before.

line.say: Its lines run on the diagonals. The knight on d5 is on none of them.

steps.caption: Each side starts with two bishops. The one on c1 stands on a dark square, the one on f1 on a light square.

line.say: Every square this bishop can reach is dark.
Black makes a waiting move.
The other bishop travels only on light squares.

steps.text: A bishop never changes the colour of square it stands on. The bishop from c1 moves only on dark squares; the one from f1 only on light squares. A piece on the other colour can never be taken by that bishop, however close it looks. Each side starts with one bishop on dark squares and one on light squares, so together they cover both colours. [V] One diagonal step changes the rank by one and the file by one, so the square colour never changes.

steps.caption: The bishop on c4 can capture the pawn on f7: the move is legal. Legal does not mean good; judging that comes later.

line.say: The bishop takes the pawn on f7. Legal does not mean wise; that needs a later skill.

steps.prompt: Explain to a friend who has never seen a bishop how to find all its moves. Write it, then open the model answer.
Your friend says: my bishop on c1 can take the rook next to it on d1. Write your reply.

steps.text: **Model answer.** Compare it with what you wrote. *Name the piece first. A bishop slides along its four diagonals as far as it likes and stops at the first piece in the way: one square short of its own piece, or on an enemy piece it captures. Its rank and file do not matter, and it keeps its colour.* Missed a part? Scroll back to the matching board.
